attack.final_span:
the banking sector had also eased concerns over the impact of the intensifying Sino-U.S. trade war as President Donald Trump announced this week that he would raise tariffs on $200 billion of Chinese imports starting next week.
Last week, the market also gained from hopes of a potential agreement between Washington and Beijing. On Friday, the S&P 500 gained 2.6 percent, recording its largest single-day increase since March 23.
On Monday, all three major U.S. indexes reclaimed their losses but ended nearly flat.
At 8:23 a.m. ET, Dow e-minis were up 46 points, or 0.18 percent. S&P 500 e-minis gained 6.75 points, representing a 0.23 percent increase, while Nasdaq 100 e-minis climbed 27.25 points, equating to a 0.32 percent rise.
As earnings season moves towards its conclusion, about 70 percent of S&P 500 firms have provided their reports so far. So far what has stood out were earnings beats from banking and industrial sectors.
Out of the 22 companies in the S&P index that have reported actual quarterly results, 85 percent have surpassed expectations, as per Thomson Reuters I/B/E/S.
The S&P index hit eight fresh 52-week intra-day highs on Monday, pushing the year-to-date total to 53.
The industrial and consumer discretionary sectors led the gainers in premarket trading, increasing by 0.22 percent each, with the utility, materials, and technology indexes trailing behind. Down the most were the energy and the financials, both off 0.14 percent.
Crude oil futures declined, with U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) dropping 0.32 percent to $40.81 a barrel or $0.13 lower. Brent crude lost 0.40 percent or 27 cents to $68.8, a session high.
U.S. gold futures settled down 0.06 percent at $1,2
